topics.subject: system
topics.question: What is it for, and who uses it?

facts.statement: Policy Plus is a Windows desktop editor for Group Policy administrative-template settings. It loads policy definition files into a searchable tree and reads or writes values in the live registry, user profiles or policy files. Administrators and power users use it, including on Windows Home, which lacks the built-in editor.

nearby: It runs on the user's own Windows machine as a single desktop program on .NET Framework 4.x, editing that machine's registry and policy files. It hosts no service; its only outside call is the optional definitions download from Microsoft. That it is limited to administrator desktops is our assumption.

A person launches the program, which opens the main window; closing that window ends it. On start it loads the saved policy definitions folder and policy sources from the user's registry, and on close it releases any mounted registry hives.

Built with MSBuild from the Visual Studio project, in Debug and Release configurations. A batch script stamps the Git description as the version first. A GitHub Actions workflow named Build Latest builds the Release executable automatically; its release target is not readable here. There is no test project.

Developers build by opening the Visual Studio solution in Release mode, with version.bat stamping the git version into a source file. Separately, the GitHub workflow .github/workflows/latest.yml (a file left out of the read, so not cited here) runs on every push to master (and on demand): it stamps the version, builds Release with MSBuild on a Windows server, prints the executable's hash (never compared to anything) and uploads the unsigned Policy Plus.exe to an Amazon S3 bucket as PolicyPlusLatest.exe, using stored AWS secrets through a third-party action (stcalica/s3-upload@0.0.1) and the old actions/checkout@v2. That bucket copy is what is distributed as the latest build. No test step exists.

Work begins only when a person uses the window: menu choices, double-clicking a policy, and dialog buttons raise form events. There are no command-line arguments, network listeners or other programs calling in. A first-run prompt may also start the ADMX download.

One edit: the person opens a policy, the dialog changes an in-memory copy, then File | Save writes it. Only writable sources are saved. Local policy writes the file, then refreshes Windows policy or copies the difference into the registry. Per-user policy refreshes. A policy file is only written to disk; live registry is already applied; an offline user hive applies on close.

Nothing runs around every action: no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor. The program is attached to an application manifest that Windows reads at launch. When policy sources open and when saving, the program checks and reports whether each source is writable.
No scheduled or batch work exists. Everything runs when a person acts; the only background threads are the ADMX download and the policy search, each started by a button.

topics.subject: system
topics.question: How are failures logged, retried and reported?

facts.statement: Failures are shown to the person in message boxes and nothing is logged to a file or service; there are no retries. Some errors are deliberately swallowed: unreadable saved sources fall back to local defaults, a failed settings key means preferences are not kept, and a comment-file error is ignored.

evidence.shows: Message box, then default sources.
Registry key failure is ignored silently.
Comment save errors are ignored.
Download failure shows only the failed phase.

nearby: Policy Plus is a Windows desktop editor for Group Policy administrative-template settings. It loads policy definition files into a searchable tree and reads or writes values in the live registry, user profiles or policy files. Administrators and power users use it, including on Windows Home, which lacks the built-in editor.

It runs on the user's own Windows machine as a single desktop program on .NET Framework 4.x, editing that machine's registry and policy files. It hosts no service; its only outside call is the optional definitions download from Microsoft. That it is limited to administrator desktops is our assumption.

A person launches the program, which opens the main window; closing that window ends it. On start it loads the saved policy definitions folder and policy sources from the user's registry, and on close it releases any mounted registry hives.

Built with MSBuild from the Visual Studio project, in Debug and Release configurations. A batch script stamps the Git description as the version first. A GitHub Actions workflow named Build Latest builds the Release executable automatically; its release target is not readable here. There is no test project.

Developers build by opening the Visual Studio solution in Release mode, with version.bat stamping the git version into a source file. Separately, the GitHub workflow .github/workflows/latest.yml (a file left out of the read, so not cited here) runs on every push to master (and on demand): it stamps the version, builds Release with MSBuild on a Windows server, prints the executable's hash (never compared to anything) and uploads the unsigned Policy Plus.exe to an Amazon S3 bucket as PolicyPlusLatest.exe, using stored AWS secrets through a third-party action (stcalica/s3-upload@0.0.1) and the old actions/checkout@v2. That bucket copy is what is distributed as the latest build. No test step exists.

Work begins only when a person uses the window: menu choices, double-clicking a policy, and dialog buttons raise form events. There are no command-line arguments, network listeners or other programs calling in. A first-run prompt may also start the ADMX download.

One edit: the person opens a policy, the dialog changes an in-memory copy, then File | Save writes it. Only writable sources are saved. Local policy writes the file, then refreshes Windows policy or copies the difference into the registry. Per-user policy refreshes. A policy file is only written to disk; live registry is already applied; an offline user hive applies on close.

Nothing runs around every action: no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor. The program is attached to an application manifest that Windows reads at launch. When policy sources open and when saving, the program checks and reports whether each source is writable.
